en: The Sūtra on the Merit of Bathing the Buddha’s Image, translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
He was together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and immeasurable great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Viśuddhamati, who reflected thus:
"By what causes and conditions do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain the pure body?"
Furthermore, he thought to himself:

"If one makes offerings while the Buddha is in the world through personal attendance and service, and another makes offerings to the relics after his parinirvāṇa—will the merit and virtue obtained by these two kinds of people be equal?"
Having formed this thought, he rose from his seat through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain the pure body?”

If one were to personally attend upon and make offerings to the Buddha while he is in the world, and another were to make offerings to his relics after his parinirvāṇa, would the merit obtained by these two types of people be equal?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! It is well that you are now able to pose such a question for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages."
"You should listen attentively; I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati addressed the Buddha, saying, "Indeed, [I shall do so]."
“World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, for the sake of seeking bodhi, cultivated in the past samādhis, precepts, concentration, patience, wisdom, kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the powers, the fearlessnesses, all Buddha-dharmas, and the knowledge of all modes; all these were entirely pure, and therefore the Tathāgata has attained a pure body."
Furthermore, they made offerings with flowers, incense, banners, and canopies;
they bathed the body of the Tathāgata with scented water;
and they covered him from above with precious parasols.
By offering various foods and drinks, drums, music, lutes, songs, and hymns in praise of the Tathāgata,
and dedicating this merit toward all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), the merit obtained will be immeasurable and boundless, until one attains unsurpassed bodhi.
Why is this? The wisdom of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; all his merit and virtue are likewise so! "Pure Wisdom!
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be two kinds of relics:
first, the Dharma-body; second, the transformation-body.

If good sons or good daughters, and others like them, make offerings to these relics, they may fashion images of the Buddha as small as a grain of barley, build stupas as small as an *āmra* fruit, with spires like needles and canopies like duckweed.
If one enshrines the Buddha’s relics, even as small as mustard seeds, within it, the merit obtained shall be equal to that when I am in the world, without any difference.
Such a person attains fifteen kinds of merit:
first, they attain a mind of pure mindfulness.
Second, they attain a mind that accords with the Dharma.
Third, they attain a mind of shame and remorse.
Fourth, they attain the vision of the Tathāgata.
Fifth, they give rise to pure faith.
Sixth, they are able to uphold the true Dharma.
Seventh, they practice according to the teachings.
Eighth, they attain the opportunity to draw near to all Buddhas.
Ninth, they take birth in the Buddha-fields according to their wishes.
Tenth, if born among humans, they are born into great families; their minds are supple and they are held in high esteem by others.
Eleventh, upon being born among humans, they immediately attain the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Twelfth, the hosts of māras cannot disturb or confuse them.
Thirteenth, during the age of the final dharma, they are able to protect the true dharma.
Fourteenth, they will always receive the constant protection and guardianship of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of the ten directions.
Fifteenth, they will swiftly achieve the accomplishment of the fivefold Dharma-body.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If, with a pure mind, one makes offerings to the relics after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa;
Or those who construct stupas and temples, as well as images of the Tathāgata;
who sweep and smear the maṇḍalas, scattering various flowers and incense upon them, and using various exquisite perfumed waters;
They bathe the Buddha-image with the most excellent of foods and drinks,
maintaining purity as they offer these in worship; they praise and revere the Buddha’s merits,
which are immeasurable and inconceivable— his wisdom and his supernormal powers.
"All skillful means have reached the other shore.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, having heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, how should sentient beings of future ages bathe the images?
We pray that the Tathāgata, for the sake of these beings, will reveal and explain this.
The Buddha said, “Viśuddhamati!

Just as when the Buddha was in the world, all sentient beings gave rise to pure minds, so too should they do after my parinirvāṇa. They should not harbor notions of grasping at emptiness; regarding all wholesome qualities, their hearts should be filled with yearning and they should never grow weary. Why is this?

In order to bring to fulfillment the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya of the Tathāgata, I have already taught you the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās; I now teach you for your sake the ritual for bathing the image, which is the most preeminent among all offerings.

“Good son! If you wish to bathe the image, you should take ox-head sandalwood, red sandalwood, *tamaraka* incense, *gongsong*, *kongqiong*, white sandalwood, *uragasāra*, *nāgapuṣpa*, camphor, aloeswood, musk, and clove—using various such exquisite fragrances as these, according to what is available—to prepare bath water. Place this in a clean vessel, first construct a square altar and arrange an exquisite seat upon it, and place the Buddha upon it;
then bathe him with these scented waters in succession.”
Having thoroughly applied various fragrant waters everywhere, one should further rinse [the image] with pure water from above.
Those who bathe the image should each take a small amount of the water used for washing the image, place it upon their own heads, and burn various kinds of incense as an offering.
"When first pouring water over the image from above and below, one should recite this verse:
'I now bathe all the Tathāgatas, The assembly adorned with pure wisdom and merit;
May the sentient beings of the five turbidities be freed from defilement, And may they realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. "
"When burning incense, one should recite this verse:
"The fragrance of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, Pervades the lands of the ten directions, ever fragrant;
May this incense smoke likewise be so, Transformed into the five kinds of bodies for myself and others."

When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, among the assembly there were immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attained the pure and stainless samādhi and immediately rose from their seats;
immeasurable devas and humans attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?”
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha said, "This sutra is named 'Bathing All Buddhas to Attain Purity of Body'; you should uphold it thus."
When this sutra had been spoken, the entire assembly was filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sutra on the Merit of Bathing the Image Spoken by the Buddha.
